newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION-HEADY FUTURE FOR CAPITAL MARKETS - UTI Securities.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-HEADY FUTURE FOR CAPITAL MARKETS - UTI Securities.

text.p: The following are excerpts of a report titled "Union
Budget 1997-98 - An Analysis" by UTI Securities Research:
HEADY FUTURE FOR CAPITAL MARKETS

The policies pertaining to direct taxes would have an electrifying impact on the domestic capital markets and on corporate finance. Capital markets and corporate finance are so tightly linked that it has been quite difficult and often frustrating to ascertain whether the former had devastated the latter or the latter had crippled the former over the last two years. The Union Budget for 1997/98 has six attractive proposals that would invigorate the former and the latter simultaneously. The Finance Minister, P.Chidambaram, has resisted the pressure and, perhaps, the temptation to abolish the much-reviled minimum alternate tax (MAT). The continuation of MAT along with the six proposals listed below make for a heady future. Quite unsurprisingly, the stock markets have responded to such an expectation with mature sobriety.
* Corporate tax rate slashed (40 percent to 35 percent; surcharge of 7.5 percent abolished).
* Tax on distributed profits at 10 percent.
* Tax on dividends (in the hands of recipients) abolished.
* Personal tax slabs shifted up and tax rates shifted down boldly (15-30-40 percent to 10-20-30 percent).
* Tax deduction at source abolished for coupons on government securities.
* Government securities included in list of investments that qualify for a higher deduction limit.

William Baumol, a highly acclaimed economist of this century, had serious reservations about companies that thrived on internal accruals. He thought that managers of such companies did not visit the capital market frequently enough to subject themselves to the discipline of the capital market. Michael Jensen, a don at the Harvard Business School and a mentor of the author of this section, did not quite admire companies that had hordes of shareholders' money. Such money solely came from operations (not from issue of equity or equity-linked securities) and yet he thought that such companies had no business to sit on large heaps of funds. Jensen thought that such companies should pay out large dividends so that share holders can make their own investment decisions. Ford Motor Company was Jensen's favourite target in this regard.

Both Baumol and Jensen would have liked to cite Indian companies as examples to support their views. Indian companies usually make more frequent visits to the capital market than any other in the world; they also pay out large dividends. Baumol and Jensen did not however use Indian companies as examples; they probably had the necessary evidence to avoid such an impulse. Indian companies are just the wrong examples!

Indian companies actually do not produce large amounts of cash flows; they, however, produce handsome earnings and pay out large dividends. Often, these dividends are paid out from funds raised in the market. Without significant internal accruals, no company can support large investments. Future cash flows of a company are results of timely investments. Investors, both domestic and foreign, had therefore turned their backs on companies that had too little cash earnings to goose internal accruals and investments.
The continuation of MAT and the tax on dividends paid out would provide the right incentives for companies to conserve cash flows by:
* reporting earnings just the way they are and

* paying just the right amount of dividends. Any company that persists with high reported earnings, high dividend pay-outs and frequent visits to the capital markets would be at a great disadvantage compared with a company that produces real cash flows from operations, pays sustainable dividends from such cash flows and makes infrequent visits to the capital markets. The advantage has shifted unambiguously to companies that create and sustain value in the long term. Baumol and Jensen would not wish to disagree.

The new tax rates and the tax slabs allow for enhanced personal savings; a greater part of such savings is likely to be invested in equity. The abolition of tax on dividends is certain to make the equity market attractive to investors, both individual and institutional, all over again. Over the last two years, principally domestic investors had lost interest. Their return to the equity markets is imminent; such a return would be obviously well-founded. It would not be built on corporate puff and froth. Their return would have a favourable impact on the secondary market; a significant improvement in liquidity; and a substantial drop in volatility.

The abolition of tax deduction at source in the context of government securities would eliminate the distortions in the yields-to-maturity of such securities. As a result, government securities may even develop a large retail base in the immediate future. The inclusion of such securities in the list of investments that qualify for a higher deduction limit would certainly enhance their attractiveness. Corporate equity offerings would have to compete vigorously with debt offerings and opportunities. There was a time when every business magazine, merchant banker and chief financial officer asserted that equity was cheaper than debt. The equity offerings in the period since 1992 were all prefaced with this assertion. They, however, did not explain if it was cheap to the company that raises it or cheap to the equity investor. Expected equity returns are set by investors and not by companies. The proposals regarding government securities would make it easier for equity investors to set the minimum expected returns from equity offerings. Corporate finance cannot ignore these developments.

The economic survey presented in the parliament on the 25th of February '97 stated that with the growing participation of virtually the entire spectrum of political opinion in the reform process, there is a good prospect that a higher growth rate would become a permanent feature of the economy.

As we had expected in our pre-budget analysis, with the passing of election distortions, the pace of economic reforms has been accelerated. The budget has done amply to revive the growth of the economy and to put it into an orbit of faster growth. The package of measures announced will have a salutary impact on the economic performance and would be supported by strong corporate performance led by demand growth and improved fundamentals.
Bottom line of corporates is expected to be boosted by one or more of the following effects of the budget and related measures:
* increase in demand driven by consumerism
* general growth in industrial activity.
* incidence of lower corporate tax rates
* deemed exports benefits to supplies made to certain projects under the procedure of international competitive bidding
* and the expected fall in the real rate of interest
We favour investments in BHEL - one of the nine gems (Navratnas) and L&T at current levels who in our view are immensely benefited out of these measures.

We feel that an increase in disposable income due to reduction in direct rates, together with reduction in excise and customs duties will have a positive impact on the demand for consumer products. We favour investments in Timex Watches, Hindustan Lever and Cadburys.
Dereservation of certain industries such as food products, biscuits hitherto reserved for SSI will help organised sector to expand and benefit. We favour investments in Britannia Industries.

The abolition of dividend taxation will make dividend yields more attractive and induce investments in value stocks. Introduction of tax concessions for retail investments in gilt securities is expected to make the debt market more vibrant besides driving the interest rates south wards.
The Finance Minister has already initiated various reforms expected to be introduced in the next one year encompasing the following areas:
* amended company law bill
* repealing of FERA
abolition of the system of ad-hoc treasury bills

We feel, taking a clue from the package of measures announced for oil exploration, that the expected reforms in the oil sector is round the corner and rationalisation of prices of petroleum products to address the burgening oilpool defecit is to follow within a short period of time.
We have summarised our views on the economy and our analysis of industries in the following pages.
ECONOMY

The Union Budget for 1997-98 has addressed the issue of sustaining and accelerating long-term economic growth in an excellent manner without compromising on economic efficiency or popular acceptance. The budget proposals has been carefully designed to augment domestic savings, make the economic environment more conducive to private domestic and foreign investment, improve the incentives for capacity augmentation in infrastructure, reduce the stifling influences on private enterprise in all sectors and improve the efficiency in resource allocation. The most striking feature of the budget is the manner in which the concerns of most of the interest groups have been addressed. Therefore, the
FISCAL MANAGEMENT:

Though the proposals do not include any drastic measure to effect fiscal correction, it attempts at bridging the fiscal deficit through innovative methods. Revenue receipts are expected to increase by over 32 billion rupees with the bulk of the increase coming from customs, excise, corporate tax, service tax and increased users charges on economic services. Therefore, the revenue deficit is expected to fall from 2.3 percent of GDP in 1996/97 (RE) to 2.1 percent in 1997/98. The Gross Fiscal Deficit is expected to fall to 4.5 percent of GDP in 1997/98 from 5 percent in 1996/97. SAVINGS:

The budget includes several measures designed to augment domestic savings. The more-than-expected reductions in personal taxation, withdrawal of surcharge and reduction in corporate taxation and rationalisation of MAT will augment savings in the household and corporate sectors. Taxation on newer categories of service providers, improved administration of income tax on the affluent evaders in metros and taxation of traders through the Estimated Income Scheme; will bring a greater number of citizens under the tax net and boost tax revenue. Opening up pension fund and health insurance to new players capable to taking on LIC and GIC and at the same time unbundling these activities from the m
INVESTMENT:

The budget includes several proposals aimed at stimulating private investment. The announcement of the new policy on oil exploration, inclusion of telecom, oil and industrial parks under infrastructure, conferring of 'deemed export' status on supplies to oil, gas and telecom sectors; will improve the investment in infrastructure. The package relating to non-infrastructural industries is also very attractive. The dereservation of 14 hitherto small-scale industries should attract domestic and foreign investment in food processing and consumer goods sector. Similarly, the changes in the Electronic Hardware Technology Park scheme permitting 50 percent sales in the dometic tarrif area, reduct
EFFICIENCY:

The budget provides sufficient thrust for improving economic efficiency in multiply ways. The reduction in peak tariffs to 40 percent reduction on tariffs on coal, chemicals, wool, paper, electronic components; will further reduces distortions. Similarly, the proposed introduction of the new law on Foreign Exchange Management, Money Laundering, and the move towards capital account convertibility; will improve the resource allocation in the economy. The eagerly awaited amendment of the Urban Land Ceiling Act which slated to be amended in the current parliament session, should improve the usage of this critical resource and thereby reduce several distortions.
SUMMING UP:

The Union Budget for 1997/98 augers very well for the long-term growth potential of the Indian economy. By providing sufficient incentives for boosting domestic investment and production, and by attempting to contain the fiscal deficit by improving the tax revenue collection, the budget provides an excellent environment for the freer play of market forces. If private economic agents respond adequately to the improved price mechanism, the Indian economy could record 7-8 percent growth in GDP during 1997/98 without stoking inflationary pressures.
